text:
Cap rate tells you about the property. Cash-on-cash tells you about your money.

Cap rate = net operating income / purchase price. It ignores financing entirely, which is useful for comparing properties but useless for judging your own return.

Cash-on-cash return = annual cash flow / total cash invested. If you put $60,000 into a deal (down payment, closing costs, rehab reserve) and it nets $8,400 in cash flow this year, that's a 14% cash-on-cash return.

Same property, different leverage, different cash-on-cash number every time. Know which question you're actually asking before you compare two deals.

text:
Lenders don't care about your gut feeling. They care about this number.

DSCR, Debt Service Coverage Ratio, measures whether a property's income can cover its own debt payments. The formula: net operating income / annual debt payments.

Example: a property nets $18,000/year after expenses. Annual debt payments run $15,000. DSCR = 1.20. Most lenders want 1.20-1.25 or higher before they'll finance it.

Below 1.0 means the property can't cover its own mortgage from operations alone. That's a red flag to catch before you're under contract, not after.

Run your DSCR before you lock the loan.

You already read blueprints better than most agents on the deal.

If you've spent years in the trades, you already know what a rehab actually costs before a contractor quotes it, which structural issues are cosmetic and which ones are expensive, and how long a scope of work really takes. That's leverage most investors are paying consultants for.

The piece that's usually missing isn't the property knowledge. It's the ownership side: how to underwrite the deal, structure the offer, and finance it so your skill turns into equity instead of just a paycheck.
